source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF, extracted text, local ICML/OpenReview HTML, and references contain no explicit code/project/visual-source link. Read-only gh searches for the exact paper title, exact arXiv ID 2512.03176, and exact-title code matches found no strict visual repository. The nearest public author repository is aliang8/interleaved_reasoning; its tree has training/evaluation Python files but no plot/figure/table/LaTeX/TikZ/PGF/SVG/notebook or paper-data source, so it is recorded only as a repository without visual source and no file is claimed as exact.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Figure 1 uses categorical Google-like yellow/blue/orange/green state fills with red/green rejection and acceptance marks; the tables are primarily black/gray, with blue citation links in Tables 5–6. No table color encodes a continuous statistic.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Body text, captions, table text, and table rules are PDF vector objects. Figure 1 is the only embedded RGB raster XObject (5648 × 2024 px, displayed 470.549 × 168.625 pt); appendix code/boxes are vector text/lines but are not Figure/Table objects.
paper_style.style_consistency: XCharter/booktabs-like tables are consistent across main results, appendices, and schema insets; grouped result tables use thin vertical separators and gray model bands, while compact reproduction lists use minimal horizontal rules. The main visual inconsistencies are Figure 1 raster typography and uncaptioned appendix/schema tables.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1 | PLANTAIN Rewind-and-Repeat After post-training an interleaved reasoning model, we apply an iterative rejection-sampling strategy for inference-time plan guidance. PLANTAIN first produces a plan as its initial intermediate response. This plan is evaluated by a human judge or an LLM autorater. If accepted, the model proceeds to generate the final answer. If rejected, the process is rewound such that the rejected plan is appended to a history of failures, and the model is re-prompted to produce a new, distinct plan. Crucially, the response generated by PLANTAIN is typically of higher quality than the response produced by a standard Think–Answer model. Additionally, subsequent thinking blocks after a rejection plan are short because the model only needs to adjust the plan rather than regenerate full reasoning. This leads to early pruning of suboptimal reasoning paths and closer alignment with true user intent.

color.semantic_mapping: Yellow marks Q; white marks Think and Plan; blue marks Response; orange marks Reject; light green marks Accept; red X and green check mark rejection and acceptance; black carries text, borders, and connectors; gray is used for shadows/anti-aliased structure.

encodings.x: Left-to-right generation order within each Think–Answer or PLANTAIN track.
encodings.y: Two categorical tracks: monolithic Think–Answer above and PLANTAIN below.
encodings.color: Node fill colors distinguish Q, Response, Reject, and Accept states.
encodings.shape: Rounded rectangles are stages; red X, green check, dots, and small illustrated agents mark rejection, acceptance, and intervention callouts.
encodings.line: Solid black connectors show the generation path and vertical callout anchors.
encodings.facet: Two horizontal tracks act as a baseline/method facet.
encodings.text: Direct node labels and callout text name Think, Plan, New Plan, Response, Reject, Accept, and example thoughts.

figures.data_and_statistics: No numeric data marks or statistical estimates are encoded. The object is a conceptual comparison of two generation protocols; the visible stages and callouts express ordering, feedback location, and rewind behavior rather than measured latency, accuracy, cost, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: This is the mechanism/interface anchor for the introduction and for Algorithms 2–3. It turns the claim that an explicit plan is an early intervention unit into a two-track visual; Table 2 measures the feedback-location comparison and Table 4 diagnoses rewind depth, while Table 1 and Table 3 report the resulting quality/efficiency evidence.
design_strengths: A page-width baseline/method pair makes the intervention point and final response visible without requiring pseudocode first.
Direct labels, Accept/Reject words, check/X symbols, and track titles redundantly encode state and sequence.
The caption supplies judge, failure-history, rewind, and short-retry semantics so the conceptual flow is interpretable outside the surrounding paragraph.
design_weaknesses: The figure is a raster XObject even though it is natively high resolution; enlarged viewing softens small labels, emoji, and thin borders compared with vector body text.
Light yellow, blue, and green fills have weak grayscale contrast; the diagram remains readable mainly through labels and symbols.
Multiple callout anchors, decorative agents, and rejection marks increase local density and would be difficult to compress into a narrow layout.
No plan length, judge cost, token count, wall-clock latency, retry budget, or uncertainty is encoded, so the figure cannot independently support quantitative claims.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use two horizontal tracks to fix the causal unit “baseline completion versus visible plan → judge → rewind/accept → final response”; pair direct stage labels with redundant status shapes and explain evaluator/history semantics in the caption. Prefer vector output and a high-contrast or textured fallback for light status fills.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1 | Interleaved reasoning generalizes beyond coding tasks, reducing latency and preserving accuracy. Plan-first decoding (Plan-Answer) substantially lowers time-to-first-response (TTFR) while maintaining or improving pass@1 accuracy compared to the standard Think–Answer baseline with a token budget of 4096. Despite being post-trained only on coding data, the learned interleaved behavior transfers effectively to math, text-to-SQL, and reading comprehension tasks.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty display: all P@1 and TTFR values are point estimates with no error bars, intervals, seed dispersion, sample denominators, or failure categories.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two Qwen3 model groups × three methods (No Thinking, Think-Answer, Plan-Answer) across MATH500, MBPP, Text-to-SQL, QuaLITY, and Average. Each benchmark has P@1↑ and TTFR↓; P@1 is shown to one decimal place and TTFR is an integer token proxy. Plan-Answer cells are bold. The PDF cell for Qwen3-8B MATH500 Think-Answer TTFR is 1587, while the surrounding p.9 prose states 2106.
tables.evidence_relation: Headline evidence for whether plan-first decoding lowers first-visible-response cost while preserving final task performance and transfers from coding-only post-training to math, text-to-SQL, and reading comprehension. Table 2 moves feedback location into the same metric contract; Table 3 changes budget and Table 4 diagnoses rewinds.
design_strengths: Grouped two-level headers align five tasks/average with the paired quality and TTFR metrics.
Repeated model groups and method order make cross-model scanning fast.
Direction arrows, one-decimal P@1, bold Plan-Answer cells, and light-gray group bands create clear hierarchy.
design_weaknesses: Eleven columns are dense at page scale and TTFR is a token proxy rather than wall-clock latency.
No denominators, repeated-run variation, failure counts, or total-token cost are visible.
The prose/table TTFR discrepancy is not explained in the caption or table body.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep a stable method × model-group × task-group contract with quality and first-response cost side by side; state token-versus-wall-clock boundaries and add denominators/dispersion when reusing it.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2 | Inference-time strategies: Plan-level feedback provides earlier and more informative supervision than answer-level feedback, yielding higher accuracy and lower TTFR. Both Best-of-N and R&R (Plan) improve over the base Plan-Answer decoding without additional training.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty display: P@1 and TTFR are point estimates; judge disagreement, repeat variation, candidate-count cost, and failure rates are absent.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two Qwen3 groups × four inference strategies (Plan-Answer, R&R (Answer), Best-of-N (5), R&R (Plan)) × five task/average groups, each with P@1↑ and TTFR↓. Best-of-N candidate count is explicit in the row label; bold cells indicate local best or better values. Values are one-decimal P@1 and integer TTFR tokens.
tables.evidence_relation: Direct mechanism/efficiency comparison for Algorithms 2–3: it places answer-level versus plan-level feedback, parallel Best-of-N, and the base Plan-Answer protocol on one task/model surface. It substantiates the claim that early plan-level supervision improves quality and first response without retraining; Table 4 supplies retry-depth diagnostics.
design_strengths: Reusing Table 1’s grouped header makes feedback location the main changed dimension.
Answer-level and plan-level rewinds are shown together, exposing the first-response difference.
Best-of-N (5), model groups, and bold local optima are explicit enough for a fast strategy scan.
design_weaknesses: Eleven columns compress strategy differences and the scope of bold comparisons is not stated in a table note.
TTFR omits judge latency, serial/parallel candidate cost, and additional generated tokens.
No calibration, denominators, repeated-run variation, or uncertainty is shown.
tables.reusable_pattern: Hold task/model columns fixed while making feedback location the row dimension; expose N and use local bolding, then report judge, candidate, and serial/parallel costs beside TTFR.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3 | Token-budget ablation: Interleaved inference achieves near-saturated accuracy at 4K tokens, highlighting efficient use of available context. While Think-Answer continues to improve with longer reasoning—reflecting redundant token usage—Plan-Answer benefits modestly from larger budgets but remains below Rewind-and-Repeat, indicating stable yet non-adaptive scaling. Rewind-and-Repeat achieves the strongest token efficiency and overall accuracy.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty display: each arrow pair is a point estimate for 4096 and 8192 token budgets; no seeds, intervals, token totals, truncation rates, or judge cost are included.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two Qwen3 groups × Think-Answer (TA), Plan-Answer, and R&R (Plan), across MATH500, MBPP, Text-to-SQL, QuaLITY, and Average. Each cell is P@1 at 4096 → 8192 tokens, shown to one decimal place; R&R (Plan) Average values are bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Budget ablation for the interleaved inference mechanism: it tests whether longer context changes the relative efficiency story established by Table 2. The table supports the near-saturation/less-redundant reasoning claim but requires text and Table 2 for TTFR and total-token interpretation.
design_strengths: The 4096 → 8192 pair is placed in the method header and repeated consistently in each cell.
Task order and model grouping match Tables 1–2, enabling across-table budget tracing.
A single bold average highlight directs attention to the declared efficiency summary.
design_weaknesses: Only P@1 is reported, so token-efficiency claims cannot be read without TTFR or total-token information.
The arrow does not state in the table whether all decoding settings other than context budget are fixed.
No denominators, seeds, or dispersion make “near saturated” a point-estimate conclusion.
tables.reusable_pattern: Encode budget as an ordered pair in each cell while preserving task/model/method order; pair it with TTFR, total tokens, and truncation/failure status in a reusable ablation.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4 | Rewind statistics. Fraction of prompts requiring plan rewinds and corresponding approval rates. On average, only 22% of plans require a rewind, and over 80% of corrections succeed within two attempts, demonstrating the efficiency of plan-level R&R.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty display: rewind fractions, approval rates, and Rewounded P@1 are point estimates; retry-depth tails, judge disagreement, and sample-size variation beyond the first-row fractions are absent.
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows are Plans needing rewind, First rewind approved, Second rewind approved, and Rewounded P@1; columns are MATH500, MBPP, Text-to-SQL, QuaLITY, and Average. The first row preserves fractions (120/500, 55/257, 60/250, 40/250) and the remaining rows are one-decimal percentages.
tables.evidence_relation: Mechanism diagnostic for Algorithm 3: it connects rejection-history depth to approval and post-rewind P@1, explaining the low-overhead plan-level control reported in Table 2. It does not provide the full final-answer distribution or end-to-end latency.
design_strengths: Rows follow the causal sequence trigger → first/second approval → post-rewind result.
Raw fractions in the first row keep benchmark denominators visible.
The short booktabs-like layout is less dense than the 11-column headline tables.
design_weaknesses: Only first and second approval rates are shown; later retries and fallback are not distributed.
The caption’s “within two attempts” is a derived sum not explicitly defined in the table.
Judge disagreement, extra tokens, and latency are not encoded, so efficiency is not independently established.
tables.reusable_pattern: Order intervention trigger, feedback depth, and corrected outcome in a compact diagnostic table; retain fractions and add complete retry-depth, fallback, token, and judge-cost columns when reusing it.

tables.label: Table 5
tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, split, deduplication, or sampling-variation display; the table gives integer dataset sizes only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns, Datasets and Dataset size. Rows: BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2024) 50; MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) (Concat 2) 50; MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) (Concat 2) 50; Multiple Solutions 26. Citation links are blue.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix reproduction inventory for the SFT stage described in A.4–A.5 and the 125 SFT traces discussed in the main text. The visible row sizes sum to 176 entries, so the distinction between dataset entries and traces is not closed by the short caption.
design_strengths: Two columns and four integer rows are easy to scan.
Blue clickable citations preserve source traceability.
Its placement directly above the identically structured RL inventory supports stage comparison.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not define whether size counts prompts, traces, or examples, nor does it give split or deduplication rules.
Color should not carry citation meaning in grayscale or print.
The sum of visible sizes and the main-text trace count require a prose clarification.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact two-column stage/dataset/size inventory with clickable citations, and define the counting unit and sampling split in a caption or note.

tables.label: Table 6
tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, split, rollout count, filtering, or sampling-variation display; the table gives integer dataset sizes only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns, Datasets and Dataset size. Rows: BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2024) 500; MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) (Concat 2) 50; MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) (Concat 2) 50; Multiple Solutions 26. Citation links are blue.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix reproduction inventory for the RL/PPO stage described in A.4–A.7. It contrasts with Table 5’s SFT list and should be read with Algorithm 4 and the A.6 parameter table; it does not support a downstream performance estimate.
design_strengths: It exactly reuses Table 5’s columns and placement, making the stage difference legible.
The 500 versus 50 BigCodeBench sizes are visible without decoding a chart.
Blue links retain dataset provenance.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not explain why BigCodeBench size changes between SFT and RL or whether sizes count prompts/rollouts.
No split, filtering, training-epoch, or sampling-temperature information is visible.
Color should not be required to identify citations in print.
tables.reusable_pattern: For adjacent training stages, reuse the same two-column inventory and add one explicit difference note for stage-specific sample counts and units.

tables.label: Parameter / Value (A.6)
tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty display; this is a fixed training-configuration inventory rather than an estimate table.
tables.data_and_statistics: Uncaptioned two-column table headed Parameter / Value with 16 visible rows: actor/critic learning rate 1 × 10−6; train/validation batch size 32/256; PPO mini/micro batch 32/16; critic micro batch 8; KL coefficient 0.001; KL loss type low variance KL; max prompt/response length 3096/2500 tokens; sampling temperature 0.7; samples per prompt 8; stable training threshold 0.05; critic warmup 0; evaluation frequency 50 steps; tensor model parallel size 2. Integer, decimal, and scientific-notation values are mixed.
tables.evidence_relation: This unnumbered table supplies the reproducibility boundary for PPO/critic/KL training and decoding lengths described in A.6–A.7, complementing Tables 5–6. It is not a result comparison and does not expose all inference-time retry parameters such as T.
design_strengths: A two-column mapping keeps 16 parameter/value pairs readable and right-column values aligned.
Booktabs-like rules avoid visual noise in a long configuration list.
Units such as tokens and steps and math notation are preserved in the values.
design_weaknesses: There is no title, table number, model/stage scope, or hardware/version field on the object itself.
Training and inference parameters are not grouped, so hierarchy and stage ownership are implicit.
Retry budget and other inference-time controls needed to reproduce Table 2 are absent.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a minimal Parameter / Value list for reproducibility, preserving units and formulas; add stage groups and a caption when parameters span training and inference.

tables.label: Table: customers
tables.uncertainty: No statistical uncertainty or aggregation is encoded; these are qualitative schema/context tables.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two unlabeled columns list CustomerID — identification of the customer (integer), Segment — client segment (text), and Currency — Currency (text). The left label “Table: customers” is bold; no numeric statistic or precision is present.
tables.evidence_relation: Qualitative schema context for the BirdSQL example: it provides field names/types around the plan and SQL shown in A.9. It supports input-context reproducibility, not a performance estimate.
design_strengths: Short field/type rows and restrained rules keep the schema subordinate to the plan/SQL example.
Field names can be checked directly against later query identifiers.
The five schema insets share a consistent visual grammar.
design_weaknesses: No column headers identify field versus description; the reader infers roles from content.
Database context is in the surrounding example box, so this inset is not self-contained.
Primary-key/foreign-key relationships are not marked.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place each qualitative schema as a named two-column inset with original field spellings and types, then reuse those identifiers verbatim in the SQL.

tables.label: Table: gasstations
tables.uncertainty: No statistical uncertainty or aggregation is encoded; these are qualitative schema/context tables.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two unlabeled columns list GasStationID, ChainID, Country, and Segment with integer/text descriptions. The left label “Table: gasstations” is bold; there are no numeric statistics or precision fields.
tables.evidence_relation: Qualitative BirdSQL schema context: it supplies the GasStationID and Country fields used by the example join/filter with yearmonth in A.9, but does not carry evaluation results.
design_strengths: Four compact rows make the join/filter fields easy to locate.
The same named-inset grammar as the other schema tables reduces visual search cost.
design_weaknesses: No explicit field/description header or key relationship is provided.
The database name and query semantics are outside the inset.
Type descriptions are text-only and do not show constraints or cardinality.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact named schema inset for join/filter tables and retain the exact identifiers needed by the subsequent query.

tables.label: Table: products
tables.uncertainty: No statistical uncertainty or aggregation is encoded; these are qualitative schema/context tables.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two unlabeled columns list ProductID — Product ID (integer) and Description — Description (text). The left label “Table: products” is bold; no numeric statistic or precision is present.
tables.evidence_relation: Qualitative schema component of the BirdSQL database shown in A.9. It is not referenced by the displayed query and therefore provides database context rather than a result or mechanism measurement.
design_strengths: The two-row inset is minimal and does not compete with the plan/SQL text.
The field/type spelling is explicit and consistent with the other schema insets.
design_weaknesses: The table’s relevance to the displayed query is not indicated.
No headers or key relationship make the object dependent on the surrounding database box.
There is no data-volume or constraint information.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep unused but contextually relevant schema tables lightweight and use the same named-inset grammar as query-critical tables.

tables.label: Table: transactions_1k
tables.uncertainty: No statistical uncertainty or aggregation is encoded; these are qualitative schema/context tables.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two unlabeled columns list nine fields—TransactionID, Date, Time, CustomerID, CardID, GasStationID, ProductID, Amount, Price—and a final italic note “Note: total price = Amount x Price”. The note is not a field; all text is black.
tables.evidence_relation: Qualitative BirdSQL schema context for A.9. Although the displayed query uses yearmonth and gasstations, this table documents the broader database schema and a derived-price relation; it does not encode benchmark statistics.
design_strengths: The longer schema remains aligned as a two-column list and preserves field names.
An italic table-tail note conveys a derived-field relation without adding a third column.
The same minimal rules and labels keep the schema family coherent.
design_weaknesses: Ten dense rows in the inset can make the italic note look like another field.
The note lacks a separate semantic marker beyond italics.
No primary/foreign-key relationships or units/cardinality are shown.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use an italic final note for a derived-field formula while keeping the field/type columns aligned and the schema identifier-preserving.

tables.label: Table: yearmonth
tables.uncertainty: No statistical uncertainty or aggregation is encoded; these are qualitative schema/context tables.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two unlabeled columns list CustomerID — Customer ID (integer), Date — Date (text), and Consumption — consumption (real). The left label “Table: yearmonth” is bold; no numeric statistic or precision is encoded.
tables.evidence_relation: This schema directly supports the A.9 plan’s 2012 Date filter, CustomerID grouping, Consumption aggregation, and SQL FROM yearmonth clause. It is qualitative input context rather than an outcome table.
design_strengths: Field/type text matches the later plan and SQL identifiers exactly.
The table is placed before the query context, reducing lookup distance.
The minimal style keeps the schema subordinate to the qualitative trace.
design_weaknesses: No headers, unit, row count, or date semantics are visible.
The meaning of Date as text requires the surrounding plan (“starts with 2012”).
No key or relationship information is encoded.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place a minimal schema inset before a SQL trace so filters, joins, and aggregates can be checked field by field against the original identifiers.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 fixes the intervention unit as an explicit plan; Table 1 establishes cross-domain quality/TTFR behavior; Table 2 varies feedback location and inference strategy; Table 3 varies token budget; Table 4 exposes rewind depth; Tables 5–6, A.6, and A.9 supply training, configuration, and qualitative input context.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Main numbered captions use “Figure/Table N |” followed by a bold title or headline sentence and then setup/comparison/finding prose. Tables 5–6 retain only short titles; the A.6 parameter and A.9 schema objects have no independent captions and depend on visible headers/labels and surrounding text.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables 1–2 use a two-level Method plus benchmark-grouped P@1↑/TTFR↓ header; Table 3 uses a budget-transition method header and task columns; Table 4 uses Metric plus benchmark columns; appendix inventories use Datasets/Dataset size or Parameter/Value; BirdSQL schema insets omit headers and pair field with description/type.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: The plan/reject/accept interface in Figure 1 maps to Algorithms 2–3, Table 2 compares plan- versus answer-level control, Table 4 diagnoses retry depth, and Tables 1/3 report cross-domain results and budget behavior. Training/data inventories remain separate from the result decision surface.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main text points to Appendix A.1/A.3/A.4/A.8/A.10 for post-training, data, qualitative traces, and evaluation context. Appendix Tables 5–6 and A.6 provide reproduction settings; A.9 schema insets provide the input context for a qualitative BirdSQL trace, but no appendix object adds uncertainty or judge calibration.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Tables use embedded XCharter-Roman/Bold with txsys/math glyphs at 9.963 pt in the main tables/schema and 10.909 pt in Tables 5–6/A.6. Figure 1 mixes raster serif-like and sans-serif-like labels at rendered estimates around 10–18 pt, so its typography is less auditable and less consistent than the tables.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Performance tables use position, arrows, bold, and gray group bands rather than color; Table 5–6 blue hyperlinks are provenance-only. Figure 1’s categorical colors are semantically redundant with labels and X/check symbols but its light fills have weaker grayscale contrast.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a two-track intervention diagram to establish visible-plan → judge → rewind/accept → response before introducing metric tables.
Keep task order, model groups, and P@1/TTFR grouped headers stable across headline, strategy, and budget tables; use direction arrows and scoped bolding.
Separate feedback-location comparisons (Table 2) from budget and retry-depth diagnostics (Tables 3–4), and keep training/data/reproduction inventories in the appendix.
Use compact two-column dataset/parameter lists and named schema insets to close reproduction and qualitative-context links without competing with result tables.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1: shortest explanation of plan → judge → rewind/accept → response.
Table 2: concentrates feedback location, strategy, P@1, and TTFR on one decision surface.
Table 1: exposes coding-only training transfer across math, text-to-SQL, and reading comprehension.
Table 4: preserves rewind denominators and approval depth needed to interpret efficiency.
Tables 5–6, A.6, and A.9 schema: complete data, configuration, and qualitative input context.
failure_patterns: Figure 1 relies on light fills and raster text, which degrade under enlargement or grayscale printing.
The dense main tables omit uncertainty, denominator/seed context, judge cost, and the wall-clock boundary of TTFR.
Short captions and uncaptioned appendix/schema objects leave dataset-size units, stage ownership, and schema column roles implicit.
The visible Qwen3-8B MATH500 Think-Answer TTFR differs between p.9 prose (2106) and Table 1 (1587); Table 5/6 size versus SFT-trace wording is also not caption-closed.
No Figure/Table directly encodes retry-budget tails, judge latency/calibration, wall-clock latency, or fallback depth.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Establish the plan as an explicit intervention unit with a direct two-track flow, then use stable grouped-header tables to tighten the quality–first-response–feedback-location–budget–retry argument and appendix lists/schema insets to supply reproduction context.
